articles.title: Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force
articles.summary:
Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (https://axonnic.com). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots.
Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA
We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly.
The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors.
When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks.
We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies.
Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension.
Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings.
So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG.
If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks!

articles.title: MacOS Golden Gate 27.3b2 Includes New Privacy Controls for Full Disk Access (and More)
articles.summary:
Remember a month ago when Apple announced, without any significant detail, that they would be changing the permission-granting UI for Full Disk Access to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action”? It’s launching today in developer beta 2 of MacOS 27.3. Chance Miller has a great overview at 9to5Mac:
In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified
toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that
level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and
photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen,
control any app on your Mac, and more.”
In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access”
into two categories:
Accessibility: Intended specifically for assistive technologies,
with permissions handled through an entitlement process.


System and App Protection Override: A new category for apps that
need to bypass certain macOS protections to control other apps
or perform automated tasks.



For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an
automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted
control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail
app, but not Messages.
macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to
request permission every time it requires access, rather than
granting it access indefinitely.
Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will
provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another
app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to
let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps
and information in the background.
I’m installing it now, but from what I’ve seen so far, these changes not only alleviate my concerns that Apple might over-tighten the screws, I actually think they add clarity and give users more, not less, control over their Macs.
 ★
articles.comment: 详细解读了macOS 27.3b2中针对全盘访问权限的全新隐私控制机制，提升了用户数据安全性。

articles.title: WSJ: ‘Nvidia’s Days as an Open Checkbook for the AI Economy Are Numbered’
articles.summary:
Robbie Whelan, Anissa Gardizy, Kate Clark, reporting for The Wall Street Journal:
In his final months as chief executive of Nvidia, Jensen Huang
was laying the groundwork to pull back the company’s approach to
backstopping the AI economy.
Now, with a finance chief at the helm who was already wary of some
deals the ousted chief forged, the startups who had been counting
on Nvidia’s support expect an even greater pullback.
Just last month, the CEOs of emerging cloud companies that buy
Nvidia chips and rent out computing power gathered in Berlin for
Nvidia’s premier European artificial-intelligence conference. In a
talk that surprised some, Huang’s message was clear: Nvidia’s days
as an open checkbook were over.
This makes sense. But how does this jibe with Nvidia moving forward on closing their preposterous $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, which Jensen Huang personally announced on September 3? That acquisition epitomizes Nvidia’s role as the “open checkbook” for the entire AI industry. In August, just before the acquisition was announced, The Information reported that Hugging Face’s annual revenue was just $150 million. Typical SaaS companies have valuations around 10× annual revenue. Let’s say Hugging Face is so super duper special that they justify 20×. That’s $3 billion. (I do not think Hugging Face is super duper special.) $13 billion is closer to 100×, which is stupid.
If the Huang era is over, Nvidia should unwind this deal.
 ★

articles.title: Ben Thompson on Nvidia
articles.summary:
Ben Thompson at Stratechery:
This led to what I termed Nvidia’s Risky Business: Nvidia
increasingly used its cash flow and credit rating to backstop and
fund the companies who were buying its chips. Bears called this
circular financing; bulls called it a necessary bridge to a future
where AI revenue paid down these companies’ debt and drove massive
upside. What is undoubtedly true is that this was the sort of
risky business that is uniquely possible for a multi-trillion
dollar company that is completely controlled by one man, who has
made an entire career of pushing the limits and making risky bets — and seeing them pay off.
It’s also a series of bets that are unlikely to continue. The
neoclouds should be very nervous about losing their patron, along
with their creditors and equity holders. The other problem is
that the revenue necessary to make all of this build-out work is
something on the order of a trillion dollars industry-wide, and
it needs to materialize sooner rather than later; if it falls
short, it’s the hyperscalers who will prioritize their own
compute first, and they will likely be seen as a safe haven for
everyone committing to spending. In that world, Nvidia’s neocloud
hedge — absent Huang’s willingness to shore the ecosystem up — is liable to turn into a millstone, with their assets flooding
the market even as the supply chain ramp-up brings ever more
supply to market.
This Nvidia crisis has made me think a lot about an item I recently posted, purely by coincidence: Charlie Munger’s 2020 take on Elon Musk and Tesla: “My thoughts are two. I would never buy it, and I would never sell it short.”
Munger used “it” in both clauses, but I think for the second one, what he really meant was that he wouldn’t short him. That he wouldn’t want to own Tesla stock (which, even today, trades at an absurd P/E ratio over 400), but he wouldn’t want to bet against Elon Musk.
I think the same thing is true for Nvidia. Nvidia in recent years made a lot of bets that investors normally wouldn’t back; but investors were willing to back Jensen Huang. Now Nvidia, the company, is left holding those risky bets and they don’t have Huang, the man, to make those bets feel like winners. I think investors are already looking at this very differently, and it’s why so many copium addicts are wailing like big babies about bringing Jensen back. Denial is the hardest stage of grief to move past.
 ★

articles.title: People will lose their jobs over GTA 6
articles.summary:
GTA 6 is about to come out, and I've seen many people online joking that they'll take the week off to play it. I'm not a big fan of GTA, but the series did leave an impression on me. The last one I played was Vice City. It was an amazing game, and I still listen to its songs. It's where I first heard "Your Love" by The Outfield. I love the game, but I don't have the luxury of playing video games the way I used to.
			
All this to say that I understand people taking time off. When Metal Gear Solid 5 came out, I didn't just take the day off. I slowly prioritized the game over the work I was supposed to be doing. I had a contract with a client who couldn't make up his mind about a project. I delivered the project, a flower subscription service, in the span of a month. He had paid a team in Ukraine $25k to hand him a broken Drupal website. I rewrote it for half the price, and he finally had the ability to manage the website on his own.
But a website isn't complete once it's delivered. There are bugs and feature requests, or the client might just change his mind about things. So he retained me for maintenance. We launched in the summer, and he couldn't have been happier. Customers flocked in, and all was well. Now it was time for maintenance.
The problem was that the client called me every day. He wanted to change everything, all the time. My expert opinion had no effect on him, he just wanted things to be different. I was getting paid for it, so I made the changes. I was constantly on the phone with him that summer. It was annoying, but that's the life of a contractor. I could have kept going, but September 1st was the release date for MGS 5.
I could have managed if I had put my mind to it. But I had already pre-ordered the game, and I had played Ground Zeroes, the prelude that came out earlier, at least a thousand times. Nothing was going to get between me and my game.
When the game came out, I stopped answering calls. Instead, I replied to emails. Whenever the title "A Hideo Kojima Game by Hideo Kojima Produced by Hideo Himself" appeared on the screen, I used the time to respond to email. Some of the work he requested was never completed, because I knew he would change his mind. The more I ignored the client's calls, the more frustrated he became, and the more of the story I missed. "Who is Skull Face again?" I didn't want to miss a second of the dialogue.
At one point, the client called and I didn't pick up, as usual. He sent a text message: "PICK UP NOW!" I knew it was serious. So I didn't pick up right away, because doing so would have made it look like I had been intentionally ignoring him. I called him back some minutes later, only to find out it was nothing urgent. The call turned into a therapy session. He was frustrated that people had flocked to the website during the grand opening, yet it had translated into few subscriptions. The website was only a few months old, mind you.
I could have given better advice, but Quiet was shooting at me from a distance, and I hadn't figured out how to win that battle yet. Besides, I was there to do technical work, not to solve his business problems. He sensed it. When he found a bug on the website, I was eager to fix it. When he wanted to discuss ways to make the subscriptions more appealing to customers, I checked out.
Eventually, he confronted me and asked whether I was all in on this business. I wasn't. I was busy thinking that the Huey character design was lazy. Why did they recycle Otacon? Couldn't they come up with something new instead of playing on our nostalgia? Anyway, I knew a couple of friends who had just started a web consulting business. They could solve business problems and do the development work, so they would be more helpful than I was. Plus, it wouldn't make sense for him to retain me while working with them.
I found them their very first client, and the client found a better team.
My consulting pattern used to be to deliver a job and then, during the maintenance phase, look for other clients. That way, I never had downtime. But this time, I used the downtime to play my game. Remember, this was 2015. $13k went so much further then than it does now.
You can imagine my disappointment when the game ended abruptly, as if the producer had been kicked out mid-development. Kojima had been ousted from Konami. Still, it was a good game. But I needed money to survive, so for my next contract, I ended up charging $18,000 for a single static HTML page.
What I mean is, as an MGS fan, I understand the GTA fans.

articles.title: ‘Meet the Anthropic Researcher Behind Silicon Valley’s “Consensual Non-Consent” Orgies’
articles.summary:
Aaron Sibarium, writing for The Free Beacon:
Paul Crowley, a cybersecurity researcher at Anthropic, is listed
as a manager of Red Means No LLC, which says that its parties are
“designed to be spaces to … ignore the ‘nos’ of others.”
Participants can use a safe word, “red,” to end an encounter but
give “default consent” to “spanking,” “wrestling,” and “light
pain” by entering the orgy, according to Red Means No’s
website. More extreme actions, including “light electricity”
and “moderate beatings,” are “permitted with negotiation,” though
“body-shaming and race-shaming … are disallowed entirely.”
The orgies have been known to attract a disproportionate number of
employees at Anthropic and OpenAI, a dynamic critics say creates
professional pressure for women in AI to attend. The criticism
spilled into public view last month after an independent AI
researcher, John Wentworth, said that he “absolutely [does]
upgrade” his assessment of AI safety experts “if I find out they
go to [Red Means No],” adding that attendance was a “strong
signal” of free thought.
I’m starting to think these Anthropic and OpenAI people are a little off.
 ★

articles.title: Irish Goodbye / French Leave / Leave the English Way
articles.summary:
Over the weekend I speculated that Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon and have “made their Irish goodbyes” from the Trump 2.0 administration (including having no representatives on the David Sacks-led PCAST). I learned today that what we Americans call an “Irish goodbye” is called a “French leave” in the U.K., and “leaving the English way” in France. The rest of Europe is split between those two, but only Americans and Canadians call it an “Irish goodbye”. (And, somehow, the Germans call it “doing a Polish one”, which is not what I would guess that phrase means.)
Anyway, I’ve got one friend who is an absolute master of the Irish goodbye. He never  says goodnight or goodbye from a group gathering. He always just disappears. And even when you know he’s going to do it, and you start keeping an eye on him to catch him in the act, the fucker slips away every time. I find it delightful, not rude.
 ★
